subject: Computer Networking
title: NTP: Keeping Clocks in Sync
description: A quick, practical guide to NTP: Keeping Clocks in Sync.

hook.text: Your phone, laptop, and server all show the exact same time. They aren't guessing — they're using NTP.

buildup.text: NTP — Network Time Protocol — synchronizes clocks across the internet to within a few milliseconds.

discovery.text: It works by exchanging timestamps with reference servers. Math accounts for network delay in each direction.

twist.text: Accurate time is critical for security. TLS certificates, log analysis, and two-factor auth all depend on it.

climax.text: Stratum 0 clocks use atomic oscillators or GPS. NTP cascades that accuracy down through layers of servers.

punchline.text: NTP keeps the digital world on the same clock.

quiz.question: Why is accurate time critical for network security?
options: Certificates, logs, and authentication depend on synchronized clocks
Faster clocks encrypt data more quickly

details.summary: NTP synchronizes computer clocks to within milliseconds of Coordinated Universal Time by exchanging timestamps with a hierarchy of time servers. Accurate time is critical for security certificates, log correlation, database replication, and distributed system coordination.
details.whyItMatters: Synchronized clocks are invisible infrastructure that everything depends on. Security protocols, logging, transactions, and distributed systems all break when clocks drift apart.
takeaways: NTP synchronizes clocks across networks to millisecond accuracy
A stratum hierarchy distributes time from atomic clock sources
Modern systems use NTP pools with multiple servers for reliability

faq.question: Why does accurate time matter for networks?
faq.answer: TLS certificates have validity windows checked against system time. Security logs must be correlated across servers using consistent timestamps. Distributed databases use timestamps for consistency. Authentication tokens expire based on time. Clock errors cause failures across all these systems.

faq.question: What is the NTP stratum hierarchy?
faq.answer: Stratum 0 devices are atomic clocks and GPS receivers. Stratum 1 servers connect directly to stratum 0 sources. Each additional stratum is one hop further from the reference clock. Most devices use stratum 2 or 3 servers. The maximum is stratum 15; stratum 16 means unsynchronized.
